control.name: Controls
control.intro: Controls set the period, the ranges and the items of a screen, and download its data. They draw only the control, with no card head or frame, so you can put them anywhere, such as a filter bar above the charts or a page header. They fill the width of their slot and are as tall as the control itself. Their background is left empty, so pick `theme` to match the background they sit on (`dark` on a dark one), and write the name screen readers read in `label`. When the value changes, the card sends a `vzb-change` event (`detail: { name, value }`), and the current value is also written on the card as `data-vzb-value`. Listen for the event and change the text of the JSON inside a chart card, and that card draws again with the new data. The selected span and the thumbs are drawn in the text color so they do not compete with the data colors of the charts.

donut-tick.when: Draws the make-up of a whole at one point in time as a donut, turns the picked slice to 12 o'clock and prints its share large in the middle. Use it to see how a total splits, such as revenue by channel or orders by payment method, and to point at one item at a time. For how much a share changed between two periods, use Waffle Flip.
rules: List 2 to 6 items in `items`, largest first, each with `name` and `value` (the raw value, such as revenue or orders). The card computes the shares. Past six slices the thin ones become hard to tell apart, so group the small items as 'Others' and put it last.

Put the name of the item to point at in `focus` (the first item when empty). Only that slice takes the first data color; the rest run from dark gray to light gray in the order of `items`. Color on one slice only makes the picked slice read first.

The picked slice always starts at 12 o'clock and runs clockwise, because a slice is easiest to size when it starts there (like the minute hand: 25% ends at 3 o'clock, 50% at 6). Ticks every 5% run around the ring, longer at 25, 50 and 75%, so the end of the slice reads against them.

Pressing a legend row or a slice (or using the keyboard) turns the ring the short way until that slice stands at 12 o'clock. It ticks over one slice at a time, and the marker at 12 o'clock flicks at each tick. The number in the middle is the share of the slice at the marker, so the slices passing by show theirs for a moment. Only the position of the ring turns; the size of each slice stays the same.

When it comes into view it turns once from the first item to the `focus` item and stops. The stopped picture alone gives the share of the picked item (in the middle) and of every item (in the legend). The tooltip of a slice gives its raw value and what share of the total that is, to one decimal.

date-picker.when: A control that picks a period (a start and an end date), or a single date, on a calendar. Use it to filter a screen by a date, such as the order date or a reference date. At rest it is one button with the current period and its number of days; press it and fields to type the dates and a month calendar rise below it.
rules: Write the starting period in `value` as YYYY-MM-DD, like `["2026-10-01", "2026-10-31"]` (empty means the 30 days up to the reference date). Write the first and last dates with data in `min` and `max`: the dates outside are dimmed and cannot be picked, so no one picks a period without data. `"today"` in place of a date is the viewer's today: for a screen of data up to today, set `"max": "today"` and leave `value` empty, and it opens on the 30 days up to today every time. The reference date is `max`, or today when it is empty. For a parameter that is a single date, set `"mode": "day"` and write one date in `value`.

List quick picks in `presets` to show them as chips under the calendar: `last7` (last 7 days) · `last30` (last 30 days) · `month` (this month) · `lastmonth` (last month) · `quarter` (this quarter) · `year` (this year) · `all` (min to max). All count from the reference date, and the chip that matches the current period is filled in the text color, so you can see which period is applied. About three chips fit on one line; more scroll sideways.

Press two dates in turn to make a period. After the first one, a pale band and the number of days follow the pointer or the focus to the date it reaches, so you know the length while you pick. On the second date the band draws from the start to the end, the button switches to the new period, the number of days rolls, and the calendar closes. The fields at the top of the calendar take the start and end dates typed in (2026-10-01, 2026.10.1, 20261001 or 10/1/2026 all read; a date that cannot be read or picked turns its field red and is not applied), so no one has to click their way to a distant date. Press the month title for the twelve months, and again for twelve years, to jump to a distant month or year. The calendar draws five weeks (a month that spans six weeks fits six into the same height, so every month is as tall), and moving to another month slides it in the direction of time.

Each change sends a `vzb-change` event. `detail.name` is `name` and `detail.value` is `["start", "end"]` (the end date included; a single date when `mode` is day). The current value is also in the card's `data-vzb-value`. The button and the calendar always share one width (300px, or the slot when it is narrower), so the button does not grow or shrink as the period changes. When the period does not fit on the button, a period in the year of the reference date drops the year, and a longer one turns into numeric dates (10/17/26). The calendar floats over the content beside it instead of pushing it away, and opens upward when there is no room below. Set `"align": "end"` to push the button to the right end of the screen.

Everything works from the keyboard: on the button, Enter, Space or the down arrow opens the calendar; in the calendar, the arrows move a day or a week, Page Up/Down a month (a year with Shift), Home/End to the start or end of the week, Enter or Space picks, and Esc closes. In the fields, Enter applies and closes. On the months and years, the arrows move, Enter picks and Esc goes back one level. The button, the band and its ends are drawn in the text color so they do not compete with the data colors of the charts.

bar-overflow.when: Bars for each period stand against one horizontal line, the same limit for every period, and only the parts above the line blink red. Use it for a trend with the same limit each period, such as a monthly budget or a monthly capacity. Do not use it for a target, where more is better.
rules: Write the periods in `labels`, their values in `values` (the same length) and one limit for every period in `limit`. Write `null` for a period with no value: its slot stays empty, since leaving the period out would shift the time axis. The name of the line (`limitLabel`, Limit when empty) and its value always sit at the right end of the line, outside the bars (the name above the line, the value below), because a label placed in a gap between bars moves with the data and is hard to find. One horizontal line means you only compare bar tops with the line to see which periods went over.

Below the line the bars are gray; only the part above it is red. The card writes the excess above each bar that went over (left out when the slot is too narrow), and pointing at a bar does not hide it, because a number that vanishes under the pointer looks like an error; the tooltip does not repeat that excess but gives the value, the limit and the share of the limit (for a bar whose excess label was left out, the tooltip adds the excess). On the line below, the card writes how many periods went over and the total excess. Keeping color for the excess makes what needs attention come first. For a rate (`pct`) the total is left out.

Use it only for limits that should not be crossed. On a target where more is better, the periods that met it would blink red like a warning. If each period has a different limit, one line cannot compare them, so do not use this card.

When the card comes into view the line is already drawn, the bars rise one by one from the left, then only the parts above the line blink three times and stop. No bar is drawn before it rises. The still frame alone shows which periods went over and by how much. Replay it with the button at the top right. When the data changes and the card redraws, it does not play from the start: the bars on screen move to the new values (a period with the same name is the same bar, a new period grows from the baseline and a removed one fades out), because a chart swapped at once does not show what changed or by how much. Even when the scale changes with the data, the bars and the limit line go straight from where they are on screen to where they end, in one move: moving the values first and the scale after makes the bars drop and come back up, which reads as bouncing. Only the bars that newly crossed the limit blink once. A monthly trend shows 13 months.

waffle-flip.when: A card that draws shares as a 100-cell waffle and flips, one by one, the cells that changed hands since the earlier period. Use it to show how much one item's share grew or shrank, such as a market share or a sales mix. It draws the change between two periods only.
rules: List 2 to 4 items in `items`, each with the raw values (units sold, sales and so on) of the `periods` (the earlier one, then the later one) in `values`. The card computes the shares and the change in points. Each period's cells add up to 100 by giving the leftover cells to the largest remainders (one cell is 1%). With a single period in `periods`, the card draws that period's cells with no period switch. When filtering leaves no item, give an empty `items` array for an empty card.

Name the item to point at in `focus` (empty means the first item). Only that item takes the first data color; the others are gray steps, from dark to light in the order listed. With color on one item only, the cells it gained or lost stand out first. There are three gray steps, so with five items or more, fold the small ones into Others.

Cells fill from the top left, column by column, starting with the focus item (one cell is 1%, and a column holds 4, 5, 10 or 20 cells depending on the arrangement). So when its share grows or shrinks, the cells flip at the end of its block, and a bracket under them gives the change in points. The big number is the focus item's share, and the badge color follows `better` (up · down).

The cells run from right under the big number to the bottom of the card, and the 100 cells share all of the width and height left. Among the arrangements (25 × 4 · 20 × 5 · 10 × 10 · 5 × 20) and the two places for the legend (right of the cells, below them), the card picks the one whose cells are closest to square and that leaves the least empty room. When the slot does not match an arrangement exactly, the cells become slightly flat or tall rectangles, because square cells would leave empty room to the right of the cells or below them. A wider, taller slot means larger cells, so the flips are easier to see.

With two periods, a period switch sits at the top right of the head. When the card comes into view, the earlier period's cells sit still, then the switch moves to the later period and only the changed cells flip one after another, while the big number and the legend shares follow the visible cells one point at a time. When all have flipped, the bracket and the badge appear and the card stops. The still frame alone shows the current share and how far it moved. Click the switch or use the left and right arrow keys to go back and forth between the two periods (going back, the cells flip in reverse, last flipped first); the switch tells which period the big number and the legend show, so the earlier values are always one step away. When the data changes and the card redraws, it does not play from the start: only the cells that differ in the picked period flip one after another, because a chart swapped at once does not show which item changed or by how many cells. The big number and the legend follow the visible cells, the change badge changes its number without blinking, and the bracket is drawn again once every cell has flipped. Items with the same names in the same order are the same cells, so when filtering keep the items and their order in `items` and change only the values (when a name or the order changes, the card draws at once instead). Hover a cell, or focus the chart and press the left and right arrow keys, to see that item's share (one decimal) and raw value for the period on screen, plus the change in points against the earlier period when the later one is on screen.

bump-race.when: A card that ranks the items in every period, joins the ranks with S-curves, and plays through the periods one at a time so the moments the order changes are visible. Use it to show how products, channels or branches moved up and down over a year, above all how far one item climbed. Ranks hide the size of the differences, so when the gaps matter, use a line chart.
rules: Put the period names in `labels` and 2 to 8 items in `items`, each with the value of every period (units sold and so on) in `values`. The card ranks each period from the largest value (`better: down` makes the smallest value rank 1). Ties follow the previous period's rank, then the listed order, and a null value takes the item out of that period's ranking and breaks its line. Draw 13 months for a monthly trend.

Name the item to follow in `focus` (empty means the first item). Only that item takes the first data color; the rest stay gray, so one path can be followed while the others cross. The label at the end of each line gives the current rank and the name, in place of a legend. Click a line or a label (on the keyboard, pick it with the up and down arrow keys and press Enter) to make that item the one in color, so any item's path can be followed the same way.

Rank 1 is at the top and periods are joined with S-curves. Labels ride on the right of the line ends and move with them, so the chart keeps room on the right for the longest label. The scrubber at the bottom is the time axis, so there is no separate period axis: the current period sits under its thumb, with the first and last periods at its ends.

When the card comes into view it waits on the first period, then moves on about every half second while the lines grow and the labels move up and down to that period's ranks, so each overtake is visible. It stops on the last period, and the still frame reads as an ordinary bump chart. Rewind, play/pause and fast-forward buttons sit to the right of the scrubber, under the label column. Play starts where the card stopped (from the start when at the end); rewind and fast-forward move one period per click, or keep moving at three times the playing speed while held and stop on the nearest period on release. Drag or click the scrubber, or press the left and right arrow keys, to move one period at a time. When the data changes and the card redraws, it does not play from the start: at the picked period, the lines on screen move to their new ranks without overshooting, because a chart swapped at once does not show whose rank changed or how. The rank on each label follows the order of the lines on screen while they move. An item with the same name is the same line; a new item appears in place and a removed one fades out where it was. If the card was playing, it plays on from that period. When `labels` change, it draws at once instead.

Hover a line, or focus the chart and press the up and down arrow keys, to see that period's rank, value and move against the previous period while the other items fade. Playback pauses while the pointer is over the chart or the chart has keyboard focus.

waterfall-walk.when: A card that joins what raised and what cut a value between a starting point and an end point, as one bar per item. On play, dots appear one by one from the level where the last bar ended and walk to the next item, the bar then rises or falls from that level, and the name and value attached to its end travel with it. Use it to tell, in order, what moved a value between two points: how the members at the start of the year became the members at the end through sign-ups and cancellations, which drivers turned last year's operating profit into this year's, or how much of revenue is left as operating profit and net income after costs. Do not use it for a trend over periods.
rules: List the items in `items` in reading order. The first item is the starting value (`{ "name": "Jan 1", "value": 720 }`), and each change is an item whose `value` is + for an increase and - for a decrease. Where the end value should stand, put `{ "name": "Dec 31", "total": true }` and leave its value out: the card computes totals so that the items and the totals never disagree. A total item in the middle stands the running total there as a subtotal (like operating profit on an income statement). The card keeps your order, so list the items in the order you explain them (for example the increases, then the decreases). Three to seven changes read well; with more, group the small ones as Other. An item whose value is null keeps its slot and passes the level on unchanged, and when the filter leaves no item, give `items` as an empty array to draw an empty state.

Total bars (the first item and every total item) stand on the floor (0) in gray, and each change bar starts at the level where the bar before it ended and moves up or down by its amount. A dotted line carries that level from bar to bar, so the eye can follow where the next bar starts; the dots fill the space between two bars at even intervals. Changes that raise the result are green and those that lower it are red; set `better` to down for a measure where lower is better, or to neutral to draw every change in the first data color. Keeping color for good and bad shows first what lifted and what cut the result. So that color is never the only cue, change values always carry a + or - sign, and the text sits above a bar that raises the level and below one that lowers it.

Names and values are printed together just outside the end each bar arrives at, not under the axis, so you can read what changed and by how much right where you are looking. Keep names short, because they sit at the bar ends (long ones are shortened). Where a slot is too narrow and the text would overlap a neighbor's text or bar, it is nudged sideways or moved further from the bar, and if there is still no room, the name and then the value are left out (the tooltip and the table keep them). Pointing at a bar does not hide its name, value or callout; the tooltip does not repeat that value but tells how it came about (for a change, where the running total moved from and to; for a total, 'first item → this total'), because a number that vanishes under the pointer looks like an error. There is no large figure under the title: a callout rising from the end bar (the last total item) gives its name, the end value, and the change against the first item (a difference instead of a percentage when the start is 0 or below). Writing the number once and giving that height to the chart makes the differences in bar height easier to see. For a flow that shows how much of the first item is left, like an income statement, set `compare` to share to print its share of the first item instead. Values below 0 are drawn under the floor line.

When the card comes into view, the first bar is already in place, and then the items move one at a time from the left. Dots appear one by one from the level where the last bar ended and walk to the next slot, and the bar rises or falls from that level with its name and value riding on its end. The value counts what is drawn so far (from +0 up to +360). At a total, the level reached pours down into a bar until it meets the floor, and when the end bar is full, the callout pops out of it and the card stops. The motion takes one step at a time in that order because it is what a waterfall chart says: each step starts where the one before it ended. The still frame reads as an ordinary waterfall chart. The replay button at the top right plays it again. When the data changes and the card redraws, it does not walk from the start: each bar moves from the level it reached to the new level without overshooting, because a chart swapped at once does not show which item changed or by how much. A step bar stays attached to where the bar before it ended, the dots, the name and value at each bar end and the bubble of the last bar follow, and the values and the change in the bubble change with them. Even when the scale changes with the data, the bar ends go straight from where they are on screen to where they end, so nothing drops and comes back up. When a step changes sign, its color and the side its text sits on follow the bar on the way. An item with the same name in the same place is the same item; when the number of items changes, the card draws its last frame at once.

Hover a bar, or focus the chart and press the left and right arrows, to see a change with its running total (before → after), or a total with its change against the first item (its share of the first item when `compare` is share), with only that bar left at full strength. Playback pauses while the pointer is over the chart or the keyboard focus is on it.

funnel-wave.when: A card for stages passed in a fixed order, like lead to won deal, that shows how much of the first stage is still left at each stage on the way to the end, counting the first stage as 100. Each stage is drawn as a water level for how many reached it, and on play the water flows in from the left, drops to the level of what is left at each boundary and runs to the end. Use it for sales stages, purchase conversion or sign-up steps when you report the share left of the start and the overall conversion. Do not use it to compare items that have no order.
rules: Write the stages in `items` in order (`{ "name": "Leads", "value": 2400 }`). A value is how many reached that stage; the card computes the share of the first stage, each stage's conversion rate (the share that moved on from the previous stage) and the overall conversion (from the first stage to the last), so do not write them. Three to six stages read well. When the filter leaves no stage, give `items` as an empty array to draw an empty state.

The stages sit side by side as cells of the same width, and the water in each cell stands at its share of the first stage. Heights are measured from the floor, so cells compare directly. A pill on the water in each cell gives that share (100% → 55% → 26% → 17% → 11%), so how much of the first 100 is left reads first, and the pill of the last stage is the conversion from the first stage to the last. A funnel is usually read as how much of the start made it to the end, so this share comes first, and the share that moved on from the previous stage (the stage conversion rate) goes in the tooltip and the table. At each boundary the water runs down in an S curve to the level of the next stage, and a 2px divider in the card background color cuts the water and its surface line so the stages part clearly. The water is one flow, so it is painted in the first color only, with each stage mixed into white by a different amount so the cells part by tone. The first stage is the lightest and the last the deepest, so the part that made it to the end shows first. On a dark background it is also mixed into white, so the yellow never turns muddy.

Under each cell are the stage value and name. Names are shortened to fit the cell, so keep them short (the tooltip and the table keep them whole). When the cells are narrow, the text steps down one size.

When it comes into view, the water flows in from the left, drops to the level of what is left at each boundary, runs to the right end, laps lightly against the end wall and settles. The value of each stage the water reaches counts up from 0, and the pill of a cell rises when the water passes its middle. The waves always die down and stop, so the water levels in the still frame are the values. The replay button at the top right plays it again. When the data changes and the card redraws, the water does not flow in from the start: in each cell it moves from where it stands to the new level without overshooting, because a chart swapped at once does not show which stage changed or by how much. The pill rides the water up and down, and the share on the pill and the value under the cell follow the water on screen. While the water in a cell is moving, the back layers rise a few pixels above it to show which cells are changing, and the front water is always at the value. A stage with the same name in the same place is the same stage; when the number of stages changes, the card draws its last frame at once.

Hover a stage, or focus the chart and press the left and right arrows, and the water in that cell ripples gently in three overlapping layers and settles in about two seconds (the two back layers are lighter versions of the same tone). The water level is the value, so the ripples stay within a few pixels and never get in the way of reading the height. The pill of that cell does not hide: it fills with the first color and grows a little, because a number that vanishes under the pointer looks like an error. The tooltip sits beside the pill and does not repeat its share; it gives the values the share is made of ('first stage value → this stage value', with an arrow for the order) and the share that moved on from the previous stage. Moving the mouse raises waves as if your hand pushed the water, and they die down. Hovering with the mouse or focusing with the keyboard pauses the flow. Screen readers get a table of stage, value, share from the previous stage and share of the first stage.

butterfly-fold.when: A butterfly chart, with the items in a center column and the values of two contrasting groups (men and women, online and offline, and so on) as bars on either side on one scale, whose two wings fold and open and, when an item is pointed at, draws a dashed line in the opposite color from the end of the shorter bar out to the length of the longer one, to show which side has more and by how much. Use it to compare the category make-up of two genders or channels, or to show where two groups part ways. When only the split between the two groups matters, use a 100% stacked bar chart; when only the size of each difference matters, use a bar chart of the differences.
rules: Put the names of the left and right groups (e.g. Women, Men) in `groups` and 2 to 10 items in `items`, each with the two groups' values in `left` and `right` (0 or more, null for no value). The items are drawn top to bottom in the order written. To compare, order them by the difference (left - right), largest first, so the left group leads at the top and the right group at the bottom. The card computes the totals, differences, ratios and shares.

Both wings share one scale (the largest value is the longest bar), because a scale per wing would make the two groups impossible to compare. Only the item names sit in the center column, which keeps the two wings close together (a wide center makes them read as two separate charts), and each value sits at the end of its own bar. The top row names the two groups with their totals at the end of each wing's side, in place of a legend.

On light, the left wing is pink-red (the second data color) and the right wing blue (the first); on dark, the left is yellow and the right white. The colors follow the groups and do not mean that one side is emphasized.

Pointing at an item draws, on the side with less, a dashed line in the opposite bar's color from the end of that bar to the length of the longer one, with a short cap at its end (like a span on a Gantt chart). Its length is the difference and its color is the side with more. This is there because the two bars of a butterfly chart grow in opposite directions, which makes their lengths hard to compare directly. A single line is used, not a fill or a box, so a value that is not there does not read as a bar and small differences still read cleanly. The line runs along the bottom edge of the bar so it does not collide with the value at the bar's end, and it is drawn only for the row pointed at, so the still frame shows only the bars at their values.

When the card comes into view, the folded wings open out to the left and right, fold once so they touch, and open again. Like a decalcomania, the wings that touch take each other's place: as they reopen, the dashed lines show on every row for about 1.3 seconds and then fade (a preview of what pointing at a row brings back). Each wing folds forward on its hinge (the edge of the name column) and the two wings move as mirror images. To read as a soft wingbeat, the motion follows a pendulum-like curve that eases out of and into every stop, and each wing bends: its root moves first and its tip follows a little later. Each row moves a little after the one above, so a wave runs from top to bottom (the top and bottom rows are never more than 0.25 seconds apart), while the two bars of a row always move together and the dashed lines appear row by row. Each bar folds horizontally in its own row and, because its length is its value, never swings past flat. The pause before starting and the rest before repeating follow the motion values (Lead, Rest); the timing of the fold is this card's own. While moving, the bars look shorter in perspective; in the still frame their lengths are the values. The values ride on the wings and fade as they fold; the names do not move. The motion ends in about 3 seconds with the wings open, and the replay button at the top right plays it again. When the data changes and the card redraws, it does not fold again: on the open wings the bars move from their length on screen to the new one without overshooting, because a chart swapped at once does not show which item changed or by how much. The values at the bar ends and the totals above change with the bars. An item with the same name is the same row, so when the order of `items` changes the rows move to their new places. A new item grows from the centre and a removed one fades out where it was. If the card was still folding, or `groups` change, it draws the open wings right away instead.

Hovering an item, or focusing the chart and pressing the up and down arrow keys, lays a faint band on that row, makes its name and both values bold, and brings up the dashed line. The tooltip does not repeat the two values; it says which side has more and by how much (difference and ratio) and, with a color swatch for each group, what share of each group's total the item is. It floats beside the row when there is room outside the wings, so it covers neither the other rows' values nor the totals (above the row when there is no room). While the pointer is over the chart or it has keyboard focus, the motion pauses.

range-slider.when: A control that picks a numeric range with two thumbs. Use it to filter a screen by a continuous value such as order value or quantity. Give it the distribution of the values and, while you drag, bars rise over the rail to show how much data falls in the range.
rules: Drag or use the arrow keys to pick between `min` and `max` in steps of `step` (empty splits the range into about 100 steps). Give the first range in `value` as `[start, end]`; empty is the whole range. The picked values sit under the thumbs and move with them, by `format`; when they meet, they merge into one 'start – end'. Press a value (or Enter on a thumb) and start and end fields open in its place to type the values: a typed value is used as it is, not snapped to `step` (commas and units are ignored, and 1.2K or 60k read too), because filtering by an exact amount is common and hard to hit by dragging. Enter or leaving the fields applies; Esc cancels.

Give `counts`, the number of records in each equal-width bin from `min` to `max`, and while you drag or move a thumb with the keys, a distribution panel rises over the rail: the bars inside the range take the text color and the count inside the range is written with `noun` (rows when empty). Picking by the range alone hides where the data piles up, which makes it easy to filter it away; at rest only the rail and the values remain, so the slider takes little room in a filter bar. A value inside a bin is counted for the share of the bin it covers, so `step` can be finer than the bin width.
Each time the value changes, the card sends a `vzb-change` event. `detail.name` is `name` and `detail.value` is `[start, end]` as numbers. The current value is also on the card as `data-vzb-value`.

Drag a thumb, press the rail to bring the nearer thumb there, or focus a thumb and press the arrow keys to move one step (Page Up and Down about ten steps, Home and End to the end). The thumbs follow like a spring; bars rise a little as they enter the range, nearest to the moving thumb first, and dip as they leave.

filter-chips.when: A control that picks several items from a fixed list as chips. Use it to filter a screen by a few names, such as channels or regions. The All chip at the front shows how many are picked.
rules: List the items in `options` and the first picks in `value` (empty picks all). Past three rows the chips go on one row that scrolls sideways, so about 8 items, all visible at a glance, fit best.

The All chip at the front (`all`; empty means "All", an empty string leaves it out) shows the number picked as a rolling number, and pressing it picks everything, or clears everything when all are picked. How many are on is always in view, so a filter is never left on by mistake.

Each time the value changes, the card sends a `vzb-change` event. `detail.name` is `name` and `detail.value` is the picked items in the order of `options`. The current value is also on the card as `data-vzb-value`.

A chip squashes a little when pressed and springs back, and when picked a check is drawn as the chip widens. Picked chips are filled with the text color so they do not compete with the data colors of the charts. Tab moves between chips and Space or Enter picks.

download-button.when: A button that downloads the data of a chart card on the screen as a file. It starts as an icon alone; hover and the formats to pick from (CSV, JSON, PNG) come out. Use it to export exactly what the controls show.
rules: Write the kind of the card to download in `target` (its `data-vzb`, e.g. `bar-overflow`). The table comes from the current JSON of the first such card on the page: `items`, else `labels` with `values` (adding `limit` and `target` as columns when present), `labels` with `series`, else the first array of objects. It reads the JSON after the controls changed it, so you get what you see.

List the formats in `formats` (`csv`, `json`, `png`; empty means all three). The CSV starts with a BOM so Excel reads non-English text correctly, and the PNG is the card as you see it at twice the size (its text may be drawn in a font installed on the device). The file name is `filename` plus the extension of the format.

An icon alone takes little room on the screen; hover it, reach it with the keyboard or press it and the button widens and the formats come out one by one. Pressing the icon again while open downloads the first format, Esc closes it, and the left and right arrows move between the formats. The widened button floats over what is next to it instead of pushing it, and when there is no room on the right it opens to the left, keeping the icon in place. To put it at the right end, as at the top right of a screen, set `align` to `end`: the icon sits at the right end and the button opens to the left.

Before downloading, the card sends a `vzb-download` event (`detail: { name, target, format, filename, rows }`). If the page calls `preventDefault()` the card makes no file, so a screen that fetches the source data from a server can use the same button.

When the file is saved, the arrow drops into the tray and turns into a check, and the format and the number of rows (for a PNG, its size) roll up next to the button and fade after 1.8 s. When there is nothing to download, the button shakes and says "No data".

select-menu.when: A control that opens a list to search and pick from when there are too many items to lay out as chips. Use it for filters with dozens of names, such as countries, regions, stores or products. At rest it is one button with what is picked; press it and a search field and the list rise below it. With about eight items, Filter Chips, which show everything at a glance, are the better fit.
rules: List the items in `options` as names or as `{ "name": "Germany", "count": 1740 }`, and the first picks in `value` (empty picks all). With `count`, each row shows how much data the item holds as a small bar (against the largest item) and a number, and the bars grow from zero as the list opens. You see where the data sits before you pick, so you are less likely to pick only items with almost no data and get an empty chart. `noun` is the word screen readers read after the number.

The button reads `all` (All when empty) when everything is picked, 'None picked' when nothing is, and otherwise the picked names in `options` order, shortened to '+the rest' when they do not fit. The badge on the right rolls to the number picked, so you never forget a filter is on. For a parameter that takes one item, set `"mode": "one"` and write one name in `value`: there is no badge or select-all row, and picking closes the list.

Typing in the search field keeps only the matching items (the rest fold away), and the matching letters turn bold with an underline that draws in. Case does not matter, and Korean names also match by initial consonants (ㄱ finds 경기, 강원, 경남…). A long list is hard to scan by eye. Select all and Clear act on the matches while you search. The list shows up to six rows and scrolls inside for more.

Each change sends a `vzb-change` event. `detail.name` is `name` and `detail.value` is the picked items in `options` order (one name when `mode` is one). The current value is also in the card's `data-vzb-value`. The button and the list always share one width (300px, or the slot when it is narrower); the list floats over the content beside it instead of pushing it away, and opens upward when there is no room below. Set `"align": "end"` at the right end of the screen.

Everything works from the keyboard. Enter, Space or the down arrow on the button opens the list with the focus in the search field; the up and down arrows (Page Up/Down for five rows) move between items and Enter picks. Esc clears the search, or closes the list when the search is empty. A picked row fills its box in the text color and draws a check, so it does not compete with the data colors of the charts.
